attribution.note: Marcus's own summary, in his own post, of how the Guardian exercise went.

semantics.note: 'Did not succeed well' matches 'didn't go well'. The 'without coding knowledge' framing comes from Marcus's surrounding text. The contract rightly treats it as unestablished: one participant was a software developer.

contract.note: Reading the line as describing substantial difficulties, not universal failure, is an ordinary plain reading. Splitting generation, debugging and the final game is fair.

evidence.note: Guardian, 11 Mar 2025. Attempt two had a broken first version, frustrating debugging, and was abandoned for Tetris. Other attempts show a square Pac-Man and a one-star clone that got basics wrong.
Same participant called it 'surprisingly easy', which tempers the picture. His bug-filled, abandoned attempt still shows difficulties, so this does not meet the contradiction condition.

reviews.rationale: The Guardian account shows real difficulties: buggy first versions, frustrating debugging, one attempt abandoned, a one-star result, and mostly mid scores. Some participants were impressed, but nothing shows consistently easy, satisfactory clones. The support condition is met.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: An unhedged 'will soon' makes this a scored forecast. The 'most or all' threshold and the 'if not already' clause are kept.

contract.note: Reading 'most' as a majority and using professional developers as a proxy is fair. The early-resolution rule matches the speaker's 'if not already'.

evidence.note: Stack Overflow 2025 survey, published July 2025: 51% of professional developers use AI tools daily. That is actual use, not planned use.
JetBrains 2025 survey of 24,534 developers: 85% regularly use AI tools. This independently corroborates majority adoption.
Methodology dates the JetBrains fieldwork to April–June 2025, shortly after the post, and describes data cleaning and weighting.

reviews.rationale: Two independent large surveys, run within months of the March 2025 post, show actual AI use by most developers (51% of professionals daily; 85% regularly). That meets the early-resolution rule for majority adoption.

attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his post.

semantics.note: A present-tense claim that the tools raise productivity, kept modest by 'somewhat'. Causal is the right kind.

contract.note: Reading autocomplete as supervised coding help and allowing a mixed result across settings are fair readings. Neither stretches 'somewhat'.

evidence.note: Google randomized trial (summer 2024 tools, 96 engineers): about 21% less time on task, though the confidence interval is wide.
METR randomized trial of early-2025 tools: experienced open-source maintainers were 19% slower with AI. It tests broad assistance, not autocomplete alone.

reviews.rationale: Controlled studies split by setting. Google's enterprise trial supports a gain, while METR found experienced maintainers in mature repos were slowed down. Per the contract, settings that disagree give a mixed result: the claim holds in some settings and not others.

attribution.note: Marcus himself asserts that Amodei's claim lacked evidence. That assertion is his, even though the prediction is Amodei's.

semantics.note: Keeps the factual core, 'without evidence'. Leaving out 'triumphantly', which is rhetoric, is fine.

contract.note: 'Without evidence' could mean no supporting observations at all, or none for the 12-month timetable. The contract flags this. Requiring an official record before declaring an absence is fair.

evidence.note: An unofficial LinkedIn transcript. The excerpt is the opening answer on scaling laws, not the coding prediction, so it neither shows nor rules out evidence for that prediction.

reviews.rationale: The packet has no official transcript or recording of the prediction and the discussion around it. The only excerpt is unofficial and covers a different part of the talk. Whether Amodei backed the prediction with evidence cannot be settled.
